stories.headline: Apple to Let iOS 27 Users Choose Third-Party AI Models Across Writing Tools, Siri, and More

stories.headline: Freshworks Cuts 11% of Workforce (~500 Jobs) as CEO Says 'Over Half of Code Is Written by AI'

key_facts.fact: Freshworks announced it would cut 11% of its workforce, about 500 jobs globally, citing AI-driven automation as a key driver. One-time restructuring charges of ~$8 million are expected.
key_facts.excerpt: Freshworks said on Tuesday it would cut 11% of its workforce, or about 500 jobs, as the business-software company grapples with an industry being reshaped by artificial intelligence.

key_facts.fact: CEO Dennis Woodside told Reuters the decision was driven by AI use in product and engineering: 'Over half of our code is written by AI,' reducing 'rote work that technology can take care of.'
key_facts.excerpt: 'Over half of our code is written by AI,' Woodside said, adding that automation had reduced 'rote work that technology can take care of.'

key_facts.fact: The cuts follow Atlassian slashing roughly 10% of jobs last month. AI tools from Anthropic and others are seen as potential existential threats to traditional software makers.

key_facts.fact: Freshworks' stock has declined about 26% in 2026. Despite the cuts, Q1 revenue rose 16% to $228.6 million, beating estimates of $223.24 million.
key_facts.excerpt: The San Mateo, California-based company's stock has declined about 26% this year... In the first quarter, revenue rose 16% to $228.6 million, compared with estimates of $223.24 million.

key_facts.fact: Layoffs.fyi reports that 92,462 tech employees globally have lost their jobs in 2026 so far. This is Freshworks' second restructuring in two years, after cutting 13% of staff in 2024.

stories.headline: Thailand Approves $12.2B Emergency Loan Decree to Cushion Hormuz-Driven Energy Crisis

key_facts.fact: Thailand's Cabinet approved a draft emergency decree to borrow up to 400 billion baht (~$12.2 billion), aimed at cushioning economic impacts from the global energy crisis and accelerating clean energy transition.
key_facts.excerpt: Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Tuesday (May 5) that the Cabinet has approved a draft emergency decree to borrow up to 400 billion baht (about US$12.2 billion), aimed at cushioning economic impacts from the global energy crisis.

key_facts.fact: PM Anutin said the decision was driven by the West Asia conflict (Hormuz disruption), which has cascaded from energy into food prices, putting significant pressure on the cost of living.
key_facts.excerpt: Anutin said the decision was driven by the ongoing West Asia conflict, which has disrupted global energy prices and economic activity, noting that the crisis has cascaded from energy into food prices.

key_facts.fact: Phase 1 provides immediate financial relief to farmers, SMEs, and low- to middle-income citizens. Phase 2 targets long-term transformation by reducing fossil fuel reliance and promoting renewables and EVs.
key_facts.excerpt: The first phase providing immediate financial relief to farmers, small- and medium-sized enterprises, and low- to middle-income citizens... The second phase seeks long-term structural transformation by reducing fossil fuel reliance, promoting renewable energy and electric vehicles.

key_facts.fact: The government aims to prevent Thailand from sliding into stagflation — high inflation combined with a slowing economy. National debt will remain below the 70% of GDP legal ceiling.
key_facts.excerpt: Anutin said the government's timely intervention is critical to prevent the Thai economy from sliding into stagflation... national debt will remain manageable and stay well below the legal ceiling of 70 per cent of gross domestic product.

key_facts.fact: The emergency decree is scheduled to be submitted to Parliament on May 14.
key_facts.excerpt: The emergency decree is scheduled to be submitted to the Parliament on May 14.

stories.headline: Trump Pauses Hormuz Reopening, US and Gulf Allies Propose New UN Resolution Threatening Iran

key_facts.fact: Trump announced Tuesday evening he was pausing the U.S. effort to guide stranded vessels out of the Strait of Hormuz to allow time for a deal to end the Iran war, while the blockade of Iranian ports remains in place.
key_facts.excerpt: U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday evening he was pausing the U.S. effort to guide stranded vessels out of the Strait of Hormuz to allow time for a deal to end the Iran war, but that the American forces' blockade of the Iranian ports would remain in place.

key_facts.fact: The US drafted a new UN Security Council resolution with Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, and Qatar that could lead to sanctions or potentially authorize force against Iran if it fails to halt attacks on shipping.
key_facts.excerpt: The United States and its Gulf allies have proposed a U.N. resolution threatening Iran with sanctions or other measures if it doesn't halt attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, stop imposing 'illegal tolls,' and disclose the placement of all mines.

key_facts.fact: Rubio called the resolution 'a real test to the U.N.' and urged China and Russia not to repeat their vetoes of a previous Hormuz resolution last month.
key_facts.excerpt: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called a U.S.-proposed U.N. resolution demanding Iran stop attacks and laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz a test of the utility of the United Nations and urged China and Russia not to repeat vetoes.

key_facts.fact: Pentagon chief Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine said Iran's attacks remain 'below the threshold of restarting major combat operations' and insist the ceasefire still holds.
key_facts.excerpt: General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Iran attacked Oman once on Monday and waged three attacks on the United Arab Emirates... However, the attacks fell 'below the threshold of restarting major combat operations at this point.'

key_facts.fact: Caine estimated 22,500 mariners on more than 1,550 commercial vessels remain stuck in the Gulf, unable to transit the strait.
key_facts.excerpt: Caine estimated 22,500 mariners embarked on more than 1,550 commercial vessels were stuck in the Gulf, unable to transit.
